title: Database Backup, Recovery and Access Control: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on backup types, point-in-time recovery with WAL/redo logs, checkpoints and ARIES, replication for high availability, and access control with GRANT/REVOKE, roles, least privilege and row-level security.

chapters.title: Backups and Recovery: The Mental Model
points: Backup types: full copies everything; incremental copies changes since the LAST backup of any type; differential copies changes since the last FULL backup
Restore chain: full only; full + differential (2 sets); full + every incremental in order (longest, most fragile)
Trade-off: incremental = smallest and fastest backup but slowest restore; differential = grows daily but restores with just 2 sets
Logical backup (pg_dump, mysqldump: SQL text, portable, slow restore) vs physical backup (file/block copy: fast, same version and platform)
RPO = how much data you can lose; RTO = how long you can be down; they decide backup frequency and the tools you pick

chapters.title: WAL, Checkpoints and Point-in-Time Recovery
points: Write-ahead logging rule: the log record reaches durable disk before the changed data page; commit = log flushed, not data pages
Redo log replays committed changes lost from memory; undo log rolls back uncommitted changes
Checkpoint flushes dirty pages and records a log position, so crash recovery starts there instead of at the beginning of the log
PITR = restore a base backup, then replay archived WAL/binlog up to a target timestamp or LSN, stopping just before the bad statement
Example (PostgreSQL): archive_command ships WAL; restore the base backup, set recovery_target_time = '2026-10-28 14:05:00', add recovery.signal, start the server
Mistake: WAL archiving not enabled before the incident, so there is nothing to replay and PITR is impossible

chapters.title: ARIES Crash Recovery Basics
points: ARIES principles: write-ahead logging, repeating history during redo, and logging undo actions with compensation log records (CLRs)
Every log record has an LSN; each page stores pageLSN, and redo skips a record when pageLSN >= its LSN
Fuzzy checkpoint saves the dirty page table and transaction table without stopping transactions

Three passes: Analysis (rebuild the dirty page table and active transactions from the last checkpoint), Redo (replay everything from the earliest recLSN, including losers), Undo (roll back uncommitted transactions)
Steal + no-force buffer policy: dirty pages of uncommitted transactions may reach disk (needs undo), and commit does not force pages to disk (needs redo)
Mistake: thinking redo only replays committed work; ARIES redoes all history first and only then undoes the losers

chapters.title: Replication for High Availability
points: Primary-replica replication ships the WAL/binlog to replicas; replicas serve reads and can be promoted if the primary fails
Synchronous (commit waits for the replica ack: zero data loss, higher latency) vs asynchronous (fast, but replication lag can lose recent commits on failover)
Failover steps: detect the failure, promote the most up-to-date replica, repoint clients, and fence the old primary to avoid split-brain
Replication is not a backup: a DROP TABLE or bad UPDATE replicates to every replica immediately, so you still need PITR and backups
Mistake: never restore-testing backups or rehearsing failover; an untested backup is not a backup

chapters.title: Access Control: GRANT, REVOKE, Roles and Row-Level Security
points: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON orders TO analyst; REVOKE INSERT ON orders FROM analyst; add WITH GRANT OPTION only when delegation is truly needed
Roles bundle privileges: CREATE ROLE readonly; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO readonly; GRANT readonly TO alice; users get roles, not direct grants
Least privilege: give each app its own role with only the needed rights, never use the owner or superuser account for the application, and revoke the default PUBLIC privileges
Row-level security (PostgreSQL): ALTER TABLE docs ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY own_rows ON docs USING (owner = current_user)
RLS gotchas: with no policy, non-owners see zero rows (default deny); table owners and superusers bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; use WITH CHECK to control writes
Mistake: REVOKE on a role does not remove privileges inherited through another role or granted to PUBLIC

chapters.title: Backup, Recovery and Security Cheat Sheet
points: Backup types: full = everything; differential = changes since last full; incremental = changes since last backup of any type
Restore needs: full / full + latest differential / full + all incrementals in order
PITR = base backup + archived WAL replayed to recovery_target_time; WAL is written before data pages
ARIES = Analysis, Redo (repeat all history), Undo (roll back losers, write CLRs); steal + no-force
HA: sync replication = no data loss but slower commits; async = fast but lag risk; replication is not a backup
Access control: GRANT/REVOKE privileges to roles, assign users to roles, apply least privilege, use RLS policies (USING / WITH CHECK) for per-row access, and restore-test regularly
